recommendation.change_summary: In 13.1, replace card_number with the HMAC PAN fingerprint (12.1) or a vendor-supported token/hash, or move the PAN call inside the CDE (Card Adapter-side vendor call). If PAN is still required, add the Fraud Hook and the FRV-1 link to the 12.2 CDE table, give it its own detokenise identity, and make the FRV-1 DPA (Backlog 4) a Phase 8 entry gate.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Keeps NFR-5 scope accurate and P2 intact; avoids an adverse QSA finding.
recommendation.issue: PAN flows to an out-of-scope service, and to FRV-1, under a credential that is not its own.
recommendation.rationale: Shared roles and unscoped PAN flows break P2/P9 and invalidate the CDE that NFR-5 assesses.
recommendation.verification: Check the Vault IAM policy so that only the Card Adapter role can call detokenise. Confirm that the 12.2 table matches the data-flow diagram, and that the QSA scoping review accepts it.

findings.statement: Section 13.1 has the Fraud Hook detokenise the full PAN, using the Card Adapter's service role, so it can send the card number to FRV-1. Section 12.1 says only the Card Adapter's identity may detokenise, and Section 12.2 lists the Fraud Hook as out of scope. As written, PAN reaches a service outside the CDE and a third party with no DPA yet (Backlog item 4), and the Card Adapter credential is shared. The CDE defined for NFR-5 therefore does not hold, and P2 and P9 are broken.
findings.title: Fraud Hook detokenises the PAN using the Card Adapter's role, which breaks the CDE boundary

With 15,000 merchants using sequential order IDs and a key namespace shared across merchants, collisions within 24 hours are near-certain, so one merchant gets another's response and the 422 mismatch rule is bypassed on cache hits.

recommendation.change_summary: In 9.2 and Section 24, change the key to idem:resp:{merchant_id}:{sha256(idempotency_key)}. Store request_hash with the response, and on a hit compare hashes and return 422 when they differ.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Prevents cross-merchant data disclosure and lost payments; FR-5 holds on every path.
recommendation.issue: The fast-path key is not scoped by merchant, and a hit returns the stored response without verifying the request hash.
recommendation.rationale: P3 requires (merchant, key) scoping, and FR-5 requires 422 on a body mismatch.
recommendation.verification: Extend the FR-5 test so that two merchants use the same key with different bodies, and a single merchant reuses a key with a different body after a cache hit. Expect separate payments and a 422.

findings.statement: The Redis key is idem:resp:{idempotency_key} with no merchant_id, and a cache hit returns the stored response without comparing request hashes. Merchants are allowed to use order or invoice numbers as keys, so collisions across merchants are likely. Merchant B could then receive merchant A's payment object (a data leak), and B's request would be silently dropped. A reused key with a different body would also return the old response instead of 422. This breaks P3 and FR-5.
findings.title: Redis idempotency fast path is not keyed by merchant and skips the body-hash check

recommendation.change_summary: In 11.2, on a timeout send a reversal for the attempt before cascading, or cascade and queue a reversal. Record late responses in attempt state rather than discarding them, and have a late approval on a non-winning attempt trigger an automatic void. Correct the duplicate-charge sentence.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Ensures at most one live authorization per payment (FR-5/FR-7) and keeps attempt records truthful (P1).
recommendation.issue: There is no reversal or void path for timed-out or late-approved attempts.
recommendation.rationale: Ambiguous outcomes have to be resolved, not discarded, to avoid duplicate holds and customer complaints.
recommendation.verification: Add a case to the FR-7 cascade simulation in which the simulator approves after 3 s. Expect a reversal sent to that acquirer and exactly one live authorization.

findings.statement: A no-response timeout is classed as retryable and triggers a cascade, and any response that arrives after the timeout is logged and discarded. An approval that arrives late at acquirer A, after B has also approved, leaves a live authorization hold on the cardholder at A. Nothing reverses it, and reconciliation will not see it until settlement, if at all. The claim that cascading cannot create a duplicate charge looks only at the ledger, not at what the cardholder sees. P1 and FR-5's 'at most one authorization' intent are not met.
findings.title: Late approvals after the 2,500 ms timeout are discarded, risking double authorizations

cluster when sustained card volume exceeds 1,500 TPS. If the HSM is unreachable

55% card share of 2,000 TPS is 1,100 TPS, below the 1,500 TPS trigger, so the design runs on one HSM in one AZ indefinitely, and a 503 classed as retryable only multiplies vault calls during the outage.

next_step.action: Benchmark HSM unwrap throughput at 2,500 TPS and document the multi-AZ and cross-region HSM topology.

recommendation.change_summary: In 12.3 and Section 24, launch with at least two HSMs in different AZs and a cross-region HSM/KEK plan. Add the Vault data store to the replication plan in 20.2. Have HSM 503 errors fail fast as non-cascadable. Size HSM throughput for detokenise plus tokenise at 2,000 TPS including cascades, and set the scale trigger by measured HSM utilisation rather than card TPS.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Card acceptance survives the loss of an AZ (NFR-3), and cards can be served after regional failover (NFR-4).
recommendation.issue: The HSM has no AZ or regional redundancy, and the scaling trigger is unreachable.
recommendation.rationale: The whole card path depends on synchronous HSM unwraps, so the HSM's availability caps NFR-3 for cards.
recommendation.verification: In a chaos test, kill the HSM in AZ-a under NFR-1 load; card authorizations should continue. A DR game day should then show card authorization succeeding in ap-southeast-3.

findings.statement: All KEKs sit in one HSM in ap-southeast-1a, and every detokenise unwraps a DEK in the HSM with no caching. Losing that AZ or that HSM stops all card tokenisation and authorization until a new HSM is restored from a daily backup. Card traffic is 55% of attempts. The trigger for adding a second HSM (1,500 card TPS) is never reached, because peak card volume is about 1,100 TPS. Section 20.2 also gives no cross-region plan for the Vault store or the HSM, so after a regional failover cards cannot be processed. This puts NFR-3 and NFR-4 at risk.
findings.title: A single CloudHSM in one AZ is a single point of failure for all card traffic, and has no regional DR

Hold the new account until it is verified (populate verified_at with a penny-drop or name check), with a 48–72 h cooling-off period, and require a second user's approval.

findings.statement: A Finance or Owner user can change the payout bank account, and the change takes effect at the next cycle. The only confirmation goes to the user who made the change. evidence.quote: Recovery point objective for authorized payments and ledger postings shall be zero, including on loss of an entire AWS region.
Replication is storagelevel and asynchronous, with typical lag under one second.
At 2,000 TPS, about 1 s of asynchronous lag means up to roughly 2,000 committed payments can be lost on regional failure, and their idempotency keys then look unused in the DR region.

next_step.action: Decide whether to accept a non-zero RPO with compensating recovery, or to fund synchronous replication.
next_step.owner: Platform architecture lead with CFO/Finance risk

recommendation.change_summary: Restate NFR-4 as RPO ≤ replication lag, with a post-failover recovery procedure: reconcile acquirer reports and settlement files to recreate lost payments, and reject or flag Idempotency-Keys first seen within N minutes before the failover. Alternatively, adopt a synchronous cross-region commit and accept its latency cost. Extend the NFR-4 game day to inject in-flight traffic.
recommendation.expected_benefit: A truthful NFR-4, and FR-5 preserved across failover.
recommendation.issue: NFR-4's zero RPO cannot be met with the chosen replication, and the post-failover idempotency gap allows double authorization.
recommendation.rationale: Either the requirement or the architecture has to change; the current state is a false promise.
recommendation.verification: Run the DR game day under load, with forced lag. Measure the payments lost, and confirm that recovery recreates them and that duplicate-key retries produce no second authorization.

findings.statement: NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings when a whole region is lost, but Aurora Global Database replication is asynchronous with up to about 1 s of lag. In-flight idempotency state is rebuilt from the payment table. Payments authorized at an acquirer but not yet replicated therefore disappear: the money is held at the acquirer with no record, and a merchant retry with the same key is treated as new, creating a second authorization. The NFR-4 game day only checks postings that were committed and replicated, so it would not catch this.
findings.title: Zero RPO on regional loss conflicts with asynchronous replication, and idempotency reconstruction allows duplicate charges

findings.statement: Section 21.1 says cascading does not affect p99 because fewer than 1% of card payments cascade. The 2025 baseline in 10.5 shows 3.8% retryable outcomes, all of which cascade, and timeout-triggered cascades already spend 2,500 ms before the second attempt. The cascade path therefore sits inside the 99th percentile, and NFR-2, which explicitly includes cascades, will fail. The NFR-2 test, which injects 3.8% retryables, should expose this, but late in Phase 9.
findings.title: The latency budget assumes cascades fall above p99, but 3.8% of card outcomes are retryable

findings.statement: Section 9.3 assumes one partition key sustains 10,000 WCU/s and counts 1 WCU per write. Response bodies of up to 4 KB make each write consume several write units, and LSI writes add more. Keeping 24 h of the largest merchant's records (about 4.7 M items a day) under one partition key with an LSI may also hit item-collection size limits. If the per-key throughput or collection limits are lower than assumed, 45% of peak traffic fails at the idempotency step. Both limits must be verified before the build.
findings.title: DynamoDB idempotency table keyed by merchant_id with an LSI concentrates the largest merchant on one hot key

recommendation.change_summary: In 9.2 and 20.3, add a lease timeout to IN_PROGRESS records. The sweeper should scan IN_PROGRESS records older than the lease: if no payment exists, delete the record or mark it retryable; if the payment is CREATED or in pre-provider states, fail or resume it, then complete the record.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Merchants are not blocked by 409s, and FR-5 holds across crashes.
recommendation.issue: No component recovers locks that have no payment, or whose payment is in CREATED.
recommendation.rationale: A crash between steps 3 and 8 is a normal failure mode.
recommendation.verification: Kill the pod at each of steps 3–7, then confirm that a retry with the same key succeeds within the lease plus one sweeper cycle.

findings.statement: IN_PROGRESS idempotency records are supposed to be recovered by the stuck-payment sweeper, but the sweeper only looks at payments in AUTHORISING. If a pod crashes after the lock but before the payment is created, or during fraud scoring or 3DS, the key stays IN_PROGRESS. The merchant then gets HTTP 409 for 24 h, or retries with a new key and risks a duplicate. This undermines FR-5 and NFR-3 under partial failure.
findings.title: The stuck-payment sweeper cannot clear idempotency locks orphaned before AUTHORISING
